posts.post_content: Who defined Pathology as the study of molecular, biochemical, functional and morphological alterations in cells, tissues and fluids during disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Thomson (1984) defined Pathology (Gr. Pathos = disease, logos = science) as the study of the molecular, biochemical, functional and morphological alterations in cells, tissues and fluids of the body during disease. Pathology links the basic subjects (anatomy, histology, embryology, physiology, biochemistry) to the clinical subjects (medicine, surgery, gynaecology).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Mallory (1914): Defined the neoplasm (new growth of cells), not pathology itself.
  • C. Celsus (AD 35): Described the first four cardinal signs of inflammation (Rubor, Tumor, Calor, Dolor), unrelated to defining pathology.
  • D. Metchnikoff (1884): Discovered phagocytosis, not the definition of pathology.

posts.post_content: The term used for the postmortem examination of a dead body specifically in veterinary medicine is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Necropsy is the term used in veterinary medicine for examination of a dead body, while Autopsy is the equivalent term used in human medicine — both describe the same procedure of examining a body after death.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Autopsy: Correct meaning but is the human-medicine term, not the veterinary term.
  • B. Biopsy: Refers to examination of tissue/fluid taken from a living animal, not a dead body.
  • D. Sequela: Refers to the final end result of a disease process, unrelated to postmortem examination.

posts.post_content: A lesion that is characteristic and diagnostic for one particular disease is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A pathognomonic lesion is diagnostic for a particular disease, e.g. haemorrhages at the base of the pulmonary artery and aorta in Bluetongue of sheep. Its presence alone can confirm the specific diagnosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Sequela: The final end result of a disease, not a diagnostic lesion.
  • C. Prognosis: An estimate of the probable outcome/severity of disease, not a lesion.
  • D. Incubation lesion: Not a standard pathological term — incubation period is the time between exposure to a cause and manifestation of disease.

posts.post_content: Naming a disease as "Bacterial pneumonia" (identifying the cause) is an example of which type of diagnosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Aetiological diagnosis names the cause of disease (e.g. "bacterial" pneumonia identifies the causative agent category).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Morphological diagnosis: Names only the lesion itself (e.g. "Pneumonia", "Enteritis") without identifying a cause.
  • C. Specific/definitive diagnosis: Relies on a pathognomonic lesion unique to one disease (e.g. corrugated intestine in Johne's disease), not simply naming a causal category.
  • D. Differential diagnosis: The process of ruling out similar diseases, typically the first step before a final diagnosis is reached.
Types of Diagnosis — Quick Reference
  • Morphological: names the lesion
  • Aetiological: names the cause ✔
  • Specific/definitive: names the disease via pathognomonic lesion
  • Differential: ruling out similar diseases

posts.post_content: The branch of pathology that applies laboratory methods at the bedside for diagnosis is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Clinical pathology applies laboratory methods at the bedside (or in-clinic) for diagnosis of disease in the live patient.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. General pathology: Deals with fundamental disease processes common to more than one tissue/organ, not bedside lab diagnostics.
  • B. Systemic pathology: Covers diseases peculiar to particular organs/systems, not the use of lab methods.
  • D. Comparative pathology: Compares disease processes between animals and humans, not a diagnostic laboratory discipline.
Other Branches
  • Special pathology: diseases caused by specific microbial pathogens
  • Nutritional/Experimental/Chemical/Toxicopathology: deficiency-excess disease / artificially produced disease / biochemical alterations / toxin-induced disease
  • Oncology: study of tumours

posts.post_content: Which of the following is classified as a predisposing (intrinsic) cause of disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Breed is an intrinsic predisposing cause of disease (e.g. heavier dog breeds are predisposed to bone disease). Predisposing causes make an animal more susceptible but do not themselves directly produce the disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bacterial infection: A definitive (extrinsic) biological/viable cause, since it is the actual disease-producing agent.
  • B. Radiation exposure: A definitive (extrinsic) physical cause.
  • D. Snake venom: A definitive (extrinsic) toxic cause (zootoxin).
Classification
  • Predisposing (intrinsic): heredity, species, breed, age, sex, colour/pigmentation ✔
  • Definitive (extrinsic): physical, chemical, biological, nutritional, immunological, toxic agents

posts.post_content: A sterile female calf, twin of a male calf, with arrested sex-organ development is called a:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A Freemartin is a sterile female calf, twin of a male, showing arrested development of the sex organs due to hormonal/cellular exchange between the twins' shared placental circulation in utero.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Hermaphrodite: Possesses both testicular and ovarian tissue simultaneously, unrelated to twinning with a male.
  • B. Pseudohermaphrodite: Has a unisexual gonad but ambiguous external genitalia — a different mechanism from freemartinism.
  • D. Teratoma: A neoplastic mass containing displaced tissue from all three germ layers, not a description of a sterile twin calf.

posts.post_content: The term for the complete absence of an organ or part of the body is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Aplasia denotes complete absence of an organ or part of the body.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Agenesia: Refers to incomplete/imperfect development of an organ, not its total absence.
  • C. Hypoplasia: The organ develops but fails to reach full adult size — it is present, just underdeveloped.
  • D. Atrophy: A decrease in size/number of cells of an organ after it has attained full growth — a postnatal acquired change, not a developmental defect.

posts.post_content: A cleft palate resulting from faulty fusion of the maxillary processes is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Palatoschisis (cleft palate) results from faulty fusion of the maxillary processes during development.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cranioschisis: A median-line cleft affecting the skull, not the palate.
  • B. Cheiloschisis: Refers to harelip (a cleft of the lip), a distinct structure from the palate.
  • D. Rachischisis: A cleft of the spinal column (also called Schistorrachis/Spina bifida), unrelated to the oral cavity.
Fissures (Median Line Clefts) — Quick Reference
  • Cranioschisis: skull
  • Cheiloschisis: harelip
  • Palatoschisis: cleft palate ✔
  • Rachischisis/Spina bifida: spinal column
  • Schistosomus/Schistocormus: abdomen / thorax-neck-abdominal wall

posts.post_content: A disease condition produced by the clinician through over- or needless medication is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Iatrogenic disease is a condition produced by the clinician through over- or needless medication or intervention.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Idiosyncrasy: Refers instead to an individual/abnormal reaction of an animal to a drug — a patient-side phenomenon, not a clinician-caused disease.
  • C. Congenital disease: A condition present at birth, unrelated to clinician-induced disease.
  • D. Sequela: The final end result of a disease process, not a cause of disease.

posts.post_content: A joint injury in which the normal anatomical relationship between bones is maintained is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A sprain is a joint injury in which the anatomical relationship between the bones is maintained.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Luxation: Also called dislocation — here the anatomical relation between bones is lost, the opposite of a sprain.
  • C. Fracture: Refers to discontinuity of a bone itself, not a joint injury.
  • D. Concussion: A violent shock, especially to the head, unrelated to joint anatomical relationships.

posts.post_content: The "nutmeg pattern" seen in the liver, with congested central veins surrounded by pale hypoxic zones, is characteristic of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The "Nutmeg liver" pattern, with congested central veins surrounded by hypoxic pale zones, is seen in chronic venous congestion (CVC), typically from long-standing central lesions such as valvular disease or myocardial failure.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Acute local active hyperaemia: Caused by increased arterial inflow due to physiological demand or inflammation (e.g. post-prandial gut) — a short-term, beneficial process without the chronic nutmeg pattern.
  • C. Active hyperaemia: An increase in arterial inflow, always acute; the nutmeg pattern is a venous/congestive phenomenon.
  • D. Hypostatic congestion: Gravity-dependent pooling of blood in the lowermost body parts, not the central-vein pattern seen in the liver.

posts.post_content: "Brown induration of the lung", associated with heart-failure cells and septal fibrosis, is most commonly caused by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Brown induration of the lung results from chronic venous congestion due to mitral valve disease: alveolar capillary distension → rupture → intra-alveolar haemorrhage → haemosiderin release → phagocytosis by macrophages (heart-failure cells) → fibrosis of the septa.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Pneumonia: Causes acute general passive hyperaemia (congestion), not the chronic haemosiderin-laden fibrotic pattern of brown induration.
  • C. Pulmonary thromboembolism: Produces acute congestion/infarction, not the slowly developing brown induration pattern.
  • D. Traumatic pericarditis: Is a cause of splenic cyanotic induration (in cattle), not brown induration of the lung.

posts.post_content: The term for haemorrhage into the vomit is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Haematemesis refers to blood in vomit.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Epistaxis: Refers to nasal (nose) haemorrhage.
  • C. Haemoptysis: Refers to blood in the sputum (coughed up from the respiratory tract).
  • D. Melena: Refers to blood present in the stools.
Site-Specific Terms — Quick Reference
  • Epistaxis: nose
  • Haematemesis: vomit ✔
  • Haemoptysis: sputum
  • Melena: stools
  • Haematuria: urine
  • Haemothorax: thoracic cavity
  • Apoplexy: brain

posts.post_content: Arrange the following in order of increasing size: Petechiae, Purpura, Ecchymoses.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Size grading of haemorrhage, from smallest to largest: Petechiae (pinpoint) < Purpura (~1 cm) < Ecchymoses (1–2 cm) < Extravasation (large area).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A: Incorrectly places Purpura before Petechiae — Petechiae is actually the smallest of the three, not Purpura.
  • C: Reverses the entire order — Ecchymoses is the largest of the three, not the smallest.
  • D: Incorrectly places Ecchymoses before Purpura — Purpura (~1 cm) is smaller than Ecchymoses (1–2 cm).

posts.post_content: A fluid with specific gravity ≥1.018 and protein content >4% is best classified as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

An exudate has specific gravity ≥1.018 and protein content >4%, is acidic, and cloudy in appearance, typically containing cells and bacteria.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Transudate: Has a much lower specific gravity (≤1.015) and protein content (<3%), and is clear/alkaline — the opposite profile described in the question.
  • C. Lymph: Not defined by these specific gravity/protein criteria; it is fluid draining from tissues via lymphatic vessels.
  • D. Chyle: A lymphatic fluid rich in emulsified fats from the intestine, not characterised by this SG/protein criterion.
Transudate vs Exudate — Quick Reference
  • Transudate: SG≤1.015, protein<3%, alkaline, clear
  • Exudate: SG≥1.018, protein>4%, acidic, cloudy ✔

posts.post_content: "Brisket disease" in high-altitude cattle is primarily driven by which initiating factor?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Brisket disease occurs in cattle above ~9000 ft due to hypoxia, leading to polycythaemia and cardiac hypertrophy, valvular incompetence, chronic venous congestion, and oedema of the brisket/jowl/neck.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Hypoproteinaemia: Causes oedema by lowering plasma osmotic pressure (e.g. malnutrition, parasitic protein loss), but is not the initiating factor in brisket disease.
  • C. Lymphatic obstruction: Causes lymphoedema (e.g. from tumour or filariasis), not the hypoxia-driven pathway of brisket disease.
  • D. Sodium retention: Contributes to oedema in conditions like congestive heart failure/nephritis, but is not the primary initiating factor at high altitude.

posts.post_content: Which feature distinguishes a true thrombus from a postmortem clot?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A true thrombus is attached to the vessel wall, composed of platelets and fibrin, and shows lamination (Lines of Zahn) — it forms in a living animal.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Presence of only fibrin: This describes a postmortem clot, not a thrombus, which contains both platelets and fibrin.
  • C. Smooth, glistening, homogenous appearance: Characteristic of a postmortem clot; a true thrombus is dry, friable, and laminated instead.
  • D. Formation after death: Describes a postmortem clot; a thrombus forms within the cardiovascular system of a living animal.

posts.post_content: Thrombosis of the anterior mesenteric artery in horses is classically associated with:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Strongylus vulgaris larval migration is the classic cause of anterior mesenteric artery thrombosis and subsequent infarction in horses.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Dirofilaria immitis: Causes parasitic embolism of the pulmonary artery in dogs, not mesenteric artery thrombosis in horses.
  • C. Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae: A cause of vegetative valvular thrombi in pigs, not mesenteric artery thrombosis in horses.
  • D. Clostridium chauvoei: Causes Black quarter, associated with a bovine mural thrombus in the left auricle, not equine mesenteric thrombosis.

posts.post_content: "The Bends" (Caisson's disease) results from embolism of which gas following rapid decompression?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Caisson's disease results from rapid decompression causing dissolved nitrogen gas to come out of solution and form bubbles/emboli.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Oxygen: Is soluble and harmless in this context — it does not form dangerous emboli during decompression.
  • B. Carbon dioxide: Also soluble and harmless during decompression, unlike nitrogen.
  • D. Hydrogen sulphide: A putrefaction gas produced by postmortem bacterial breakdown, unrelated to Caisson's disease.

posts.post_content: In the pathogenesis of infarction, coagulation necrosis typically becomes evident at approximately what time after arterial blockage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Coagulation necrosis is typically evident around 24 hours after blockage (red infarct stage), with RBC lysis and transition to a pale infarct occurring by about 72 hours, followed eventually by scar formation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 1 hour: Too early — at this stage the tissue is still undergoing ischaemia/capillary dilation and hypoxia, before coagulation necrosis is established.
  • C. 72 hours: This is when RBC lysis occurs and the lesion transitions to a pale infarct, not when coagulation necrosis first becomes evident.
  • D. 1 week: By this time the lesion is progressing toward inflammation and scar formation, well beyond the initial coagulation necrosis stage.

posts.post_content: An infarct is classically described as:

_aimcq_options.text: Cone-shaped, apex at the point of vessel obstruction

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

An infarct is classically cone-shaped, with the apex at the point of vessel obstruction and the base at the periphery of the organ, reflecting the branching pattern of the end artery supplied.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Spherical, uniform throughout: Does not reflect the wedge/cone-shaped distribution dictated by the vascular supply territory.
  • C. Linear, following the vessel course: Infarcts affect the tissue territory supplied distal to the blockage, forming a cone/wedge, not a thin line along the vessel.
  • D. Irregular with no consistent shape: Incorrect — the cone shape is a consistent, classic feature of infarcts.

posts.post_content: The most common type of blood maldistribution shock, caused by endotoxin (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria, is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Septic shock, caused by endotoxin (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria, is the most common type of blood maldistribution shock.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Anaphylactic shock: A maldistribution shock, but caused by Type I hypersensitivity/mast-cell degranulation (allergen, drug, vaccine), not bacterial endotoxin.
  • B. Neurogenic shock: A maldistribution shock caused by autonomic discharge/venous pooling (trauma, electrocution, fear), not endotoxin.
  • D. Cardiogenic shock: Results from failure of the heart to pump adequately (e.g. myocardial infarction), an entirely different category from maldistribution shock.

posts.post_content: Which of the following is the earliest and most common reversible response of a cell to injury?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Acute cell swelling is the earliest and most common reversible change following cell injury, occurring when cells fail to maintain ionic and fluid homeostasis; grossly the organ appears pale, turgid and heavier.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Necrosis: Represents irreversible cell death, not a reversible early response.
  • C. Apoptosis: A programmed, irreversible form of single-cell death, not a reversible degenerative change.
  • D. Dysplasia: A disordered pattern of tissue maturation, not an acute reversible response to a single injurious insult.

posts.post_content: Which group of animals is uricotelic and therefore predisposed to gout?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Birds are uricotelic (uric acid, an insoluble end-product of nitrogen metabolism), predisposing them to gout when excretion fails.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Mammals: Are ureotelic — they excrete nitrogen as soluble urea, which does not readily precipitate as uric acid/urate crystals in tissue.
  • C. Fish and D. Amphibians: These groups are typically ammonotelic (excreting soluble ammonia), not uricotelic, and gout is not a characteristic disease of these groups in this context.

posts.post_content: Visceral gout is characterized grossly by:

_aimcq_options.text: White chalky deposits on serosal surfaces

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Visceral gout presents as white chalky urate deposits on the kidney, heart serosa, mesentery, air sacs, and peritoneum.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Tophi around the joints: This is characteristic of articular gout, not visceral gout.
  • C. Yellow fatty liver: Describes hepatic lipidosis, a completely separate condition from gout.
  • D. Blue-black skin discolouration: Not a feature of gout; this description fits pigment disorders such as argyria or plumbism.

posts.post_content: Type II glycogen storage disease (Pompe's disease) results from deficiency of which enzyme?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Pompe's disease (Type II glycogenosis) results from deficiency of lysosomal α-glucosidase, and occurs in cattle, dogs, cats and sheep.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Glucose-6-phosphatase: Deficiency causes Type Ia von Gierke disease (in humans/pups), not Pompe's disease.
  • C. Amylo-1,6-glucosidase: Deficiency causes Type III Cori-Forbes' disease (dogs, cats), a different glycogenosis.
  • D. β-galactosidase: Deficiency causes GM1 gangliosidosis, a lipid storage disease, not a glycogen storage disease.
Glycogenoses — Quick Reference
  • Type II Pompe's: lysosomal α-glucosidase ✔
  • Type Ia von Gierke: glucose-6-phosphatase
  • Type III Cori-Forbes: amylo-1,6-glucosidase

posts.post_content: Which special stain is used to demonstrate fat in the liver and is PAS negative?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Oil Red O stains fat red and is PAS negative; it requires cryostat sections since routine xylol tissue processing dissolves fat.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Prussian blue: Demonstrates haemosiderin (iron pigment), not fat.
  • C. von Kossa stain: Demonstrates calcium deposits (black colour), not fat.
  • D. Congo Red: Demonstrates amyloid deposits (with apple-green birefringence under polarised light), not fat.

posts.post_content: An Hsp-peptide complex (as opposed to either component alone) is significant because it:

_aimcq_options.text: Elicits an MHC I-restricted CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell response

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Heat shock proteins act as chaperones of antigenic peptides — the combined Hsp-peptide complex (not either component alone) elicits an MHC I-restricted CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell response, relevant to anti-cancer immunity.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Causes immediate cell death: Heat shock proteins function as protective chaperones during injury, not as direct killers of the cell.
  • C. Directly neutralises free radicals: Free radical scavenging is instead performed by agents like Vitamin E, glutathione, and ceruloplasmin, not HSPs.
  • D. Prevents chromatin condensation: Chromatin condensation is a feature of apoptosis, an unrelated process to HSP-peptide immune signalling.

posts.post_content: Which of the following acts as a scavenger against free-radical cell injury?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vitamin E, along with cystine/methionine, glutathione, and ceruloplasmin, scavenges free radicals that would otherwise attack membrane lipids and nucleic acids.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Vitamin K: Involved in prothrombin/clotting factor synthesis, not free radical scavenging.
  • C. Thromboxane A2: A vasoconstrictor derived from arachidonic acid metabolism, unrelated to antioxidant defence.
  • D. Bradykinin: A kinin-system mediator causing increased vascular permeability and pain, not an antioxidant.

posts.post_content: Necrosis is best defined as:

_aimcq_options.text: Death of cells/tissue in a living, vascularised animal
Deposition of calcium in dead tissue

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Necrosis (Gr. Nekrosis = deadness) is the death of cells or tissue occurring in a living, vascularised animal, and unlike apoptosis, it elicits an inflammatory response.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Programmed single-cell death without inflammation: This describes apoptosis, the opposite of necrosis in terms of inflammatory response.
  • C. Reversible cell swelling: Describes acute cell swelling, a reversible degenerative change, not necrosis (irreversible cell death).
  • D. Deposition of calcium in dead tissue: Describes dystrophic calcification, a secondary process that can occur in necrotic tissue, not the definition of necrosis itself.

posts.post_content: The extrinsic (receptor-mediated) pathway of apoptosis is initiated by activation of which caspase?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The extrinsic pathway begins when Fas ligand cross-links with the Fas receptor, recruiting FADD and activating caspase-8, which then activates the executioner caspase cascade.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Caspase-3 and B. Caspase-6: These are executioner caspases, activated downstream by either pathway, not the initiator of the extrinsic pathway.
  • D. Caspase-9: This is the initiator caspase of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, not the extrinsic (receptor) pathway.

posts.post_content: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, which protein family becomes dominant under cellular stress to promote apoptosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Under cellular stress, the pro-apoptotic Bak/Bax/Bim proteins predominate over the anti-apoptotic Bcl-2/Bcl-x proteins, increasing mitochondrial permeability, releasing cytochrome C, which binds Apaf-1 and activates caspase-9.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bcl-2/Bcl-x: These are anti-apoptotic proteins that protect the cell — they are suppressed/overridden under stress, not dominant.
  • C. FLIP: Inhibits caspase-8 activation in the extrinsic pathway, unrelated to the mitochondrial pathway.
  • D. FADD: An adaptor protein in the extrinsic (Fas) pathway, not the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway.

posts.post_content: The most characteristic histological feature of apoptosis is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Chromatin condensation, forming a crescent/semilunar shape beneath the nuclear membrane, is the most characteristic feature of apoptosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cell swelling: A feature of reversible cell injury (and of necrosis), not the hallmark of apoptosis, which instead shows cell shrinkage.
  • C. Neutrophilic infiltration: Occurs with necrosis due to the inflammatory response; apoptosis is specifically defined by the absence of inflammation.
  • D. Coagulation necrosis: A pattern seen in ischaemic necrosis (e.g. infarcts), not in apoptosis.

posts.post_content: Carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) causes hepatic injury primarily via which mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Formation of CCl₃ free radical causing lipid peroxidation

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CCl₄ is converted to the CCl₃ free radical, which causes lipid peroxidation, decreased protein synthesis, and fatty liver — an example of indirect chemical injury via reactive metabolites.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Direct binding to sulphydryl groups: This is the mechanism of mercuric chloride (HgCl₂), a direct-acting chemical toxin, not CCl₄.
  • C. Osmotic cell lysis: Not the mechanism of CCl₄ toxicity, which is centred on free-radical-mediated lipid peroxidation.
  • D. Complement-mediated cytolysis: An immune-mediated injury mechanism, unrelated to CCl₄'s metabolic activation pathway.

posts.post_content: The onset of rigor mortis is primarily attributable to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

ATP depletion is the mechanism driving rigor mortis, which typically has an onset of 1–8 hours and resolves in 20–30 hours.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lactic acid accumulation alone: Lactic acid does accumulate postmortem, but it is the resulting ATP depletion — not lactic acid itself — that is the direct mechanism of muscle rigidity.
  • C. Bacterial putrefaction: A separate, later postmortem change (anaerobic saprophytic breakdown), not the cause of rigor mortis.
  • D. Haemoglobin imbibition: A separate postmortem change producing pinkish staining of vessel endothelium, unrelated to muscle stiffening.

posts.post_content: Rigor mortis characteristically starts in which muscle groups first?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rigor mortis starts in the most active muscles — heart, eyelids, head/neck — then progresses: head/neck → forelimbs → trunk → hindlimbs, resolving in the same order.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Hindlimb muscles: These are the last muscles affected in the sequence, not the first.
  • B. Trunk muscles: Affected after the head/neck and forelimbs, in the middle of the sequence.
  • D. Forelimb muscles: Affected second in sequence, after the head/neck region, not first.

posts.post_content: Which feature differentiates postmortem autolysis from necrosis?

_aimcq_options.text: Autolysis shows a focal distribution; necrosis is uniform
Autolysis shows no inflammatory reaction; necrosis shows inflammation
Autolysis occurs before death; necrosis after death
Autolysis is always due to bacteria

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

PM autolysis shows no inflammatory reaction and a uniform tissue distribution, whereas necrosis occurs adjacent to living tissue and elicits inflammation, with a diffuse/focal distribution.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A: This reverses the actual pattern — autolysis is uniform throughout the tissue, while necrosis is diffuse/focal adjacent to living tissue.
  • C. Autolysis occurs before death; necrosis after death: Incorrect — autolysis is strictly a postmortem event, while necrosis occurs in a still-living, vascularised animal.
  • D. Autolysis is always due to bacteria: Autolysis is primarily driven by the body's own autolytic enzymes; bacterial action is responsible for the separate process of putrefaction.

posts.post_content: The postmortem black/green discolouration of the intestine known as pseudomelanosis coli is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Pseudomelanosis coli is a postmortem discoloration due to iron sulphide formation from putrefactive bacterial action on haemoglobin, and is not related to true melanin pigment (hence the prefix "pseudo").

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bile pigment imbibition: Produces yellow staining near the gall bladder, a separate postmortem change from pseudomelanosis coli.
  • C. Haemosiderin deposition: An in-vivo pathological pigment accumulation process, not the postmortem mechanism responsible for pseudomelanosis coli.
  • D. Melanin accumulation: Explicitly ruled out by the name "pseudo"-melanosis — the black colour mimics melanin but is actually iron sulphide.

posts.post_content: Which type of gangrene characteristically shows NO line of demarcation and results from intestinal displacement (e.g. volvulus, intussusception)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Moist gangrene results from intestinal displacement (intussusception, volvulus, incarceration) and shows soft, reddish-brown to black tissue with foul odour and NO line of demarcation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Dry gangrene: Typically affects extremities (tail, ears, legs, udder) from toxins/frostbite, and characteristically SHOWS a line of demarcation — the opposite of what's described.
  • C. Gas gangrene: Caused by anaerobic Clostridium species in necrotic tissue, with gas bubbles as the distinguishing feature, not primarily linked to intestinal displacement.
  • D. Senile gangrene: Not one of the three classic types (dry, moist, gas) described in this classification scheme.

posts.post_title: Confirming a Foal Was Born Alive
posts.post_content: The medico-legal "lung float test", used to determine whether a foal was born alive, works on which principle?

_aimcq_options.text: Floating lungs indicate the presence of air, i.e. the animal breathed
Sinking lungs indicate the animal breathed
Floating lungs indicate the animal did not breathe
The test evaluates gastric milk/curd content

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

In the lung float test, lungs that float in water contain air, indicating the animal breathed and was therefore born alive.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Sinking lungs indicate the animal breathed: This is the reverse of the actual principle — sinking (non-buoyant) lungs indicate no air was present, i.e. the animal did not breathe.
  • C. Floating lungs indicate the animal did not breathe: Also the reverse of the correct interpretation.
  • D. The test evaluates gastric milk/curd content: This describes the separate suckle test, not the lung float test.

posts.post_content: Inhalation of stone (silica) dust leading to nodular pulmonary fibrosis is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Silicosis results from stone/silica dust inhalation, causing nodular fibrosis with concentric hyalinised collagen layers, and predisposes to tuberculosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Anthracosis: Caused by coal dust, and is inert and only mildly fibrogenic — it does not cause the nodular fibrotic pattern of silicosis.
  • C. Siderosis: Caused by iron dust, producing brown-black granules within macrophages (seen in horses/mules/dogs), not stone dust.
  • D. Chalicosis: Caused by cement dust exposure, a different pneumoconiosis from silicosis.
Pneumoconioses — Quick Reference
  • Coal = Anthracosis
  • Stone = Silicosis ✔
  • Iron = Siderosis
  • Cotton = Byssinosis
  • Asbestos = Asbestosis
  • Cement = Chalicosis

posts.post_content: Ferruginous bodies in the lung, which can predispose to mesothelioma, are associated with which pneumoconiosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Asbestosis causes interstitial fibrosis, and characteristic ferruginous bodies (macrophage attempts to digest fibres), which can progress to mesothelioma.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Anthracosis: An inert, mildly fibrogenic condition from carbon dust with no association with ferruginous bodies or mesothelioma.
  • B. Silicosis: Causes nodular fibrosis and predisposes to TB, but is not associated with ferruginous bodies or mesothelioma.
  • D. Byssinosis: Caused by cotton dust exposure, unrelated to ferruginous bodies or mesothelioma risk.

posts.post_content: Melanin is synthesised from tyrosine via which intermediate, catalysed by tyrosinase?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Melanin is formed from the oxidation of tyrosine → DOPA → melanin by the copper-dependent enzyme tyrosinase, in melanocytes.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Bilirubin and C. Biliverdin: These are haemoglobin breakdown products in the bile pigment pathway, unrelated to melanin synthesis.
  • D. Haematoidin: An iron-free haemoglobin breakdown pigment, also unrelated to the tyrosine-melanin pathway.
DOPA Reaction

DOPA-positive cells = melanocytes; DOPA-negative pigment-laden macrophages = melanophores.

posts.post_content: The "wear and tear pigment" associated with brown atrophy of post-mitotic cells such as neurons and cardiomyocytes is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Lipofuscin is the "wear and tear" or "aging" pigment, a brown residue of free radical lipid peroxidation accumulating in post-mitotic cells, producing brown atrophy.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Melanin: A protective black pigment formed from tyrosine oxidation, unrelated to cellular aging/wear-and-tear.
  • B. Haemosiderin: A golden-brown iron-derived pigment from haemoglobin breakdown, not the aging pigment.
  • D. Ceroid: The early/pathological form of lipofuscin (associated with Vitamin E deficiency and cachexia), a related but distinct entity from the classic "wear and tear" lipofuscin.

posts.post_content: The highest normal amount of splenic haemosiderin is found in which species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The horse normally has the highest amount of splenic haemosiderin, while the dog has the least.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Dog: Has the least normal splenic haemosiderin among domestic species, the opposite of what's asked.
  • C. Cat and D. Pig: Neither represents the species with the documented highest normal splenic haemosiderin level — that distinction belongs to the horse.

posts.post_content: Haemosiderin is demonstrated histochemically by which reaction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Haemosiderin is demonstrated by the Prussian blue reaction, producing an insoluble blue-black ferric ferrocyanide complex.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Von Kossa stain: Demonstrates calcium (black), not iron-containing haemosiderin.
  • B. Congo Red stain: Demonstrates amyloid (apple-green birefringence), unrelated to haemosiderin.
  • D. Oil Red O: Demonstrates fat (red), not iron pigment.

posts.post_content: Metastatic calcification is characterized by calcium deposition in normal tissue occurring in association with:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Metastatic calcification occurs in otherwise normal tissue and is associated with hypercalcaemia (>12 mg/dL), e.g. from parathyroid tumours, bone tumours, excess vitamin D, or renal disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Normal blood calcium levels: This describes dystrophic calcification, not metastatic calcification, which specifically requires elevated blood calcium.
  • C. Necrotic tissue only: Also describes dystrophic calcification (which occurs in dead/necrotic tissue); metastatic calcification instead occurs in normal tissue.
  • D. Hypocalcaemia: The opposite of the actual association — metastatic calcification is linked to hypercalcaemia, not low blood calcium.

posts.post_content: The von Kossa stain demonstrates calcium deposits as which colour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The von Kossa stain demonstrates calcium deposits as black, whereas H&E stains calcium blue.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Red: This is the colour fat is stained by Oil Red O, not calcium by von Kossa.
  • B. Blue: This is how calcium appears with routine H&E staining, not with the specific von Kossa method.
  • D. Green: Associated with apple-green birefringence of Congo Red-stained amyloid under polarised light, not von Kossa-stained calcium.

posts.post_content: In haemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice, the van den Bergh reaction is typically:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Haemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice shows a raised unconjugated bilirubin, giving an indirect van den Bergh reaction.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Direct: Characteristic of obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice with raised conjugated bilirubin, not haemolytic jaundice.
  • C. Biphasic: Characteristic of toxic (intrahepatic) jaundice, where both conjugated and unconjugated fractions rise.
  • D. Negative: Incorrect — the van den Bergh reaction is positive (indirect pattern) in haemolytic jaundice, not negative.
Jaundice — Quick Reference
  • Haemolytic: Indirect vdB
  • Toxic (intrahepatic): Biphasic vdB
  • Obstructive (posthepatic): Direct vdB, clay-coloured greasy faeces

posts.post_content: Obstructive jaundice predisposes to prolonged clotting time primarily because of:

_aimcq_options.text: Vitamin K malabsorption from lack of bile reaching the gut

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

In obstructive jaundice, bile fails to reach the gut, impairing fat-soluble Vitamin K absorption (needed for prothrombin synthesis), which prolongs clotting time.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Excess bilirubin toxicity to platelets: Not the mechanism described in obstructive jaundice's coagulopathy; the issue is Vitamin K malabsorption, not direct platelet toxicity.
  • C. Increased fibrinolysis: Not the primary mechanism linked to obstructive jaundice.
  • D. Hypercalcaemia: Unrelated to obstructive jaundice or its effect on clotting time.

posts.post_content: Clay-coloured, greasy, foul-smelling faeces are characteristic of which type of jaundice?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice is characterized by clay-coloured, greasy, foul-smelling faeces due to lack of bile pigment reaching the intestine.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Haemolytic: Faeces are instead intensely yellow with no unusual smell, since bile flow to the gut is unimpaired.
  • B. Toxic (intrahepatic): Faeces are typically normal in appearance in this form of jaundice.
  • D. Physiological neonatal: Not one of the three pathological jaundice categories (haemolytic/toxic/obstructive) discussed, and not characterised by clay-coloured stools.

posts.post_content: Dystrophic calcification typically begins around which nidus?

_aimcq_options.text: A phosphate nidus from dead tissue

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Dystrophic calcification begins with calcium deposition around a phosphate nidus derived from dead tissue, forming calcium soaps, and occurs with normal blood calcium levels.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. A calcium carbonate crystal: Not the described nidus mechanism; the process begins from a phosphate nidus in dead tissue.
  • C. An intact collagen fibre: Dystrophic calcification is linked to necrotic/dead tissue, not intact healthy collagen.
  • D. A cholesterol crystal: Not the primary nidus described for dystrophic calcification pathogenesis.

posts.post_content: Type III (hepatogenous) photosensitisation, the commonest type in herbivores, results from impaired hepatic excretion of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Type III (hepatogenous) photosensitisation results from impaired hepatic excretion of phylloerythrin, a chlorophyll metabolite, and is the commonest form seen in herbivores (e.g. due to Lantana camara, Tribulus terrestris toxicity).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Hypericine and C. Fagopyrin: These are directly ingested plant photodynamic pigments involved in Type I (primary) photosensitisation, not the hepatogenous type.
  • D. Uroporphyrin: Accumulates in Type II photosensitisation from inherited porphyrin metabolism disorders, not the hepatogenous Type III mechanism.

posts.post_content: Which is an example of Type I (primary) photosensitisation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Type I (primary) photosensitisation results from ingested/absorbed photodynamic plant pigments reacting directly with UV light, e.g. hypericine from Hypericum, fagopyrin from buckwheat.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bovine congenital porphyria: An example of Type II photosensitisation (inherited porphyrin metabolism defect), not Type I.
  • C. Leptospirosis and D. CCl4 toxicity: Both cause hepatic damage leading to Type III (hepatogenous) photosensitisation via impaired phylloerythrin excretion, not Type I.

posts.post_content: Neurons and cardiac myocytes belong to which category of cells with respect to proliferative capacity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Neurons and cardiac/skeletal myocytes are permanent cells, which cannot regenerate once lost.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Labile cells: Divide continuously (e.g. epidermis, bone marrow), unlike neurons/cardiac cells, which do not divide.
  • B. Stable cells: Divide only on demand (e.g. liver, bone), a category distinct from the non-dividing permanent cells.
  • D. Totipotent cells: Not a proliferative-capacity category used in this classification (labile/stable/permanent); it refers to a cell's developmental potency.

posts.post_content: Hindlimb atrophy in horses caused by Strongylus larvae occluding the femoral artery is an example of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

This is an example of angiotrophic (ischaemic) atrophy, resulting from vascular occlusion (Strongylus larvae in the femoral artery) leading to hindlimb atrophy in horses.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Disuse atrophy: Results from immobility/inactivity (e.g. plaster-cast immobilisation), not vascular occlusion.
  • B. Neurotrophic atrophy: Results from nerve injury (e.g. recurrent laryngeal nerve injury), not arterial occlusion.
  • D. Endocrine atrophy: Results from hormonal changes (e.g. castration → prostate atrophy), not a parasitic vascular cause.

posts.post_content: Which of the following best describes metaplasia?

_aimcq_options.text: Reversible replacement of one adult cell type by another within the same germinal layer
Uncontrolled proliferation with no useful function
Complete failure of an organ to develop

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one adult cell type by another, within the same germinal layer — a "double-edged sword" that may precede cancer.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Irreversible malformed tissue maturation: This describes dysplasia, not metaplasia — metaplasia is reversible.
  • C. Uncontrolled proliferation with no useful function: Describes neoplasia (per Mallory's definition), an entirely distinct process from metaplasia.
  • D. Complete failure of an organ to develop: Describes aplasia, a developmental anomaly unrelated to metaplasia.

posts.post_content: When dysplasia involves the full thickness of stratified squamous epithelium, it is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Full-thickness dysplasia of stratified squamous epithelium is termed "carcinoma in situ" (preinvasive carcinoma) — it is potentially reversible if the inciting stimulus is removed.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Metaplasia: A reversible change of cell type within the same germ layer, a precursor process but not equivalent to full-thickness dysplasia.
  • B. Anaplasia: A loss of cellular differentiation seen in malignant neoplasms, but not itself the specific term for full-thickness epithelial dysplasia.
  • D. Hyperplasia: An increase in cell number, a distinct process from the disordered maturation of dysplasia.

posts.post_content: The fifth cardinal sign of inflammation, "Functio laesa" (loss of function), was added by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The first four cardinal signs (Rubor, Tumor, Calor, Dolor) were described by Cornelius Celsus (AD 35); the fifth, "Functio laesa", was added by Rudolf Virchow (AD 1858).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cornelius Celsus: Described the original four signs (Rubor, Tumor, Calor, Dolor), not the fifth.
  • C. Julius Cohnheim: Described the vascular changes/sequence of acute inflammation, not the cardinal signs.
  • D. Elie Metchnikoff: Discovered phagocytosis, unrelated to the cardinal signs of inflammation.

posts.post_content: Who described the sequence of vascular events in acute inflammation (momentary vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Julius Cohnheim (1839–1884) described the vascular changes in acute inflammation: momentary vasoconstriction → histamine-driven vasodilation → increased blood flow → new capillary bed opening → increased vascular permeability.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Elie Metchnikoff: Discovered phagocytosis, not the vascular sequence of inflammation.
  • C. Rudolf Virchow: Added the fifth cardinal sign of inflammation, unrelated to describing vascular events.
  • D. Cornelius Celsus: Described the original four cardinal signs, not the vascular event sequence.

posts.post_content: In the sequence of leucocyte emigration, "Rolling" of leucocytes along the endothelium is mediated by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rolling is mediated by selectins, following margination, and preceding adhesion (mediated by integrins/ICAM), emigration, and chemotaxis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Integrins: Mediate the subsequent adhesion step, not rolling.
  • C. ICAM: An adhesion molecule involved in the firm adhesion step (with integrins), not rolling.
  • D. Chemokines: Drive the later chemotaxis step (directed migration), not the rolling step.

posts.post_content: Phagocytosis was discovered in 1884 by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Elie Metchnikoff discovered phagocytosis in 1884.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Julius Cohnheim: Described the vascular events of inflammation, not phagocytosis.
  • C. Rudolf Virchow: Added the fifth cardinal sign of inflammation (functio laesa), unrelated to the discovery of phagocytosis.
  • D. Cornelius Celsus: Described the original four cardinal signs of inflammation in antiquity, long before the discovery of phagocytosis.

posts.post_content: A firmly attached fibrinous membrane associated with underlying coagulation necrosis is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A diphtheretic membrane is firmly attached and associated with coagulation necrosis of the underlying tissue.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Pseudomembrane: Is only loosely attached and lacks the necrosis found beneath a diphtheretic membrane — this is the opposite feature.
  • C. Granulation tissue: A vascular/fibroblastic repair tissue formed during wound healing, unrelated to fibrinous exudate membranes.
  • D. Serosanguinous exudate: A blood-tinged serous fluid, not a firmly attached fibrinous membrane.

posts.post_content: Formation of pus (suppurative inflammation) requires which combination of factors?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Suppurative (purulent) inflammation requires necrosis, neutrophils, and proteolysis together to form pus, typically caused by pyogenic bacteria such as Staph, Strep, E. coli.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Fibrin deposition alone: Characteristic of fibrinous inflammation, not suppurative/purulent inflammation.
  • C. Mucus-secreting epithelium: Characteristic of catarrhal inflammation, not pus formation.
  • D. Eosinophilic infiltration: Associated with parasitic/allergic responses, not the neutrophil-driven process of pus formation.

posts.post_content: Compared to histamine, leukotrienes are approximately how much more potent in increasing vascular permeability?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Leukotrienes are approximately 1000 times more potent than histamine. PAF is even more potent, at 100–10,000 times histamine.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 10 times: This is roughly the relative potency of bradykinin compared to histamine, not leukotrienes.
  • B. 100 times: Underestimates the potency; leukotrienes are around 1000 times more potent, not merely 100.
  • D. Equally potent: Incorrect — leukotrienes are dramatically more potent than histamine, not equivalent.

posts.post_content: Activation of Hageman factor (Factor XII) triggers which of the following systems?

_aimcq_options.text: Kinin, Clotting, Fibrinolytic, and Complement systems

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Hageman factor (XII), activated on contact with collagen/platelets, triggers the Kinin, Clotting, Fibrinolytic, and Complement systems together.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only the clotting system: Underestimates its reach — Hageman factor also activates the kinin, fibrinolytic, and complement systems, not just clotting.
  • C. Only the complement system: Also too narrow, omitting clotting, kinin, and fibrinolytic activation.
  • D. Only the fibrinolytic system: Again too narrow, omitting the other three systems it activates.

posts.post_content: Which complement component functions as the major opsonin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

C3b is the major opsonin of the complement system, coating pathogens to enhance their phagocytosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. C3a: Functions as an anaphylatoxin (triggering histamine release), not an opsonin.
  • B. C5a: Functions as both an anaphylatoxin and a chemotactic factor, not primarily as the opsonin.
  • D. C5b-9: Forms the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC), causing direct cell lysis, not opsonisation.

posts.post_content: The classic cheese-like (caseating) granuloma is associated with which disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A grey-white, cheese-like caseating granuloma centre is the classic finding in Tuberculosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Blastomycosis: Classically produces pyogranulomatous inflammation (granulomatous exudate plus neutrophils), not the classic caseating pattern of TB.
  • C. Aspergillosis: A fungal cause of granulomatous inflammation, but not classically associated with the caseating (cheese-like) pattern specific to TB.
  • D. Actinomycosis: Causes granulomatous/pyogranulomatous lesions, but the classic caseating description is specifically linked to TB.

posts.post_content: Inflammation caused by viral infection is typically characterized by which cell infiltrate, distinct from bacterial inflammation?

_aimcq_options.text: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages — no neutrophils or suppuration

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Viral inflammation is characterized by lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, with no neutrophils and no suppuration, unlike typical bacterial (pyogenic) inflammation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Predominantly neutrophils: This describes bacterial (pyogenic) inflammation, the opposite of the typical viral pattern.
  • C. Eosinophils only: Characteristic of parasitic/allergic reactions, not typical viral inflammation.
  • D. Mast cells only: Not the characteristic infiltrate of viral inflammation, which is dominated by mononuclear cells.

posts.post_content: A basophilic inclusion body indicates:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Basophilic inclusion bodies indicate that viral replication is complete, whereas acidophilic inclusion bodies indicate ongoing replication.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Ongoing viral replication: This is the meaning of an acidophilic inclusion body, not a basophilic one — the two staining patterns have opposite meanings.
  • C. Bacterial infection: Inclusion bodies are a viral phenomenon, not associated with bacterial infection.
  • D. Fungal infection: Also unrelated — inclusion bodies specifically reflect intracellular viral replication activity.

posts.post_content: Which inflammatory cell is described as the "microphage of Metchnikoff" and represents the first line of cellular defence?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The Neutrophil, termed the "microphage of Metchnikoff", is the first line of cellular defence — an early, pyogenic responder from the bone marrow that cannot reproduce locally.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Macrophage: Represents the second line of cellular defence, arriving later (48–72h), not the first.
  • B. Lymphocyte: Also arrives late (48–72h) and is involved in cell-mediated/humoral immunity, not the early first-line response.
  • D. Eosinophil: Involved in the late parasite/allergy response, not the early first-line defence role of the neutrophil.

posts.post_content: Unlike neutrophils, macrophages at the site of inflammation are unique in that they:

_aimcq_options.text: Can reproduce locally at the inflammatory site

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Macrophages, arising from monocytes and appearing late (48–72h), are unique among inflammatory cells in that they can reproduce locally at the site of inflammation, functioning as the "second line of cellular defence".

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Arrive first, within minutes: This describes neutrophils, not macrophages, which arrive later (48–72h).
  • C. Are non-phagocytic: Incorrect — macrophages are highly phagocytic, one of their key functions.
  • D. Are derived directly from lymphocytes: Incorrect — macrophages are derived from monocytes, not lymphocytes.

posts.post_content: Kupffer cells, part of the mononuclear phagocyte system, are located in which organ?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages of the liver.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Lung: Home to alveolar macrophages, not Kupffer cells.
  • C. Skin: Home to the Langhans' cell, a different mononuclear phagocyte system member.
  • D. Bone: Home to osteoclasts, the specialised bone-resorbing mononuclear phagocyte, not Kupffer cells.
Mononuclear Phagocyte System — Quick Reference
  • Liver — Kupffer cells ✔
  • Nervous system — Microglial cells
  • Lung — Alveolar macrophages
  • Skin — Langhans' cell
  • Bone — Osteoclasts

posts.post_content: Mirror-image (owl-eye) nuclei in a giant cell are characteristic of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The Reed-Sternberg cell, seen in Hodgkin's disease, shows characteristic mirror-image (owl-eye) nuclei.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Langhans' giant cell: Shows a horseshoe/peripheral arrangement of 50–100 nuclei, not the mirror-image owl-eye pattern.
  • C. Touton giant cell: Seen in xanthomas, with a distinct wreath-like nuclear arrangement, not the owl-eye pattern of Reed-Sternberg cells.
  • D. Foreign body giant cell: Shows nuclei scattered without the specific mirror-image arrangement of Reed-Sternberg cells.

posts.post_content: Fever, as an endogenous pyrogenic response, is primarily mediated by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

IL-1 and TNF act as endogenous pyrogens, resetting the hypothalamic thermostat and driving fever.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Histamine and serotonin: Increase vascular permeability early in inflammation, but are not the primary endogenous pyrogens.
  • C. C3a and C5a: Function as anaphylatoxins and chemotactic agents, not the principal pyrogenic mediators.
  • D. PDGF and EGF: Growth factors involved in wound healing/tissue repair, unrelated to fever generation.

posts.post_content: Which of the following are considered the major acute-phase proteins in fever?

_aimcq_options.text: C-reactive protein (CRP) and Serum amyloid protein (SAP)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The major acute-phase proteins induced during fever are C-reactive protein (CRP) and Serum amyloid protein (SAP).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Fibrinogen and albumin: Fibrinogen is an acute phase protein, but albumin is actually a negative acute phase protein (decreases); this pairing is not the correct "major" answer.
  • C. Haptoglobin and transferrin: Haptoglobin is an acute phase protein, but transferrin is a negative acute phase reactant, not part of the classic major pair.
  • D. IL-1 and IL-6: These are cytokines that drive the acute phase response, not the acute phase proteins themselves.

posts.post_content: Which protein is central to both the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints of the cell cycle?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

p53 governs both the G1/S (restriction point) and G2/M checkpoints, preventing damaged or incomplete DNA from passing to daughter cells.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cyclin D: Regulates progression through G1, and is overexpressed in many cancers, but is not the central checkpoint regulator for both G1/S and G2/M like p53.
  • C. PDGF: A growth factor promoting fibroblast/smooth muscle migration and angiogenesis, not a cell-cycle checkpoint protein.
  • D. VEGF: A growth factor driving angiogenesis, unrelated to cell-cycle checkpoint control.

posts.post_content: Which growth factor primarily induces fibrosis by promoting collagen/fibronectin synthesis and inhibiting collagen degradation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

TGF-β, produced by platelets, endothelium, T cells, and macrophages, induces fibrosis by promoting collagen/fibronectin synthesis while inhibiting most epithelial growth.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. PDGF: Promotes migration/proliferation of fibroblasts, macrophages, and smooth muscle plus angiogenesis, but is not the primary fibrosis-inducing factor described.
  • C. VEGF: Primarily drives angiogenesis, not fibrosis via collagen synthesis.
  • D. EGF: A mitogen for epithelial cells and fibroblasts, not specifically the fibrosis-driving factor.

posts.post_content: Healing of a clean, sutured surgical incision (first intention) typically forms a mature scar by approximately:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Healing by first intention (clean sutured wound) forms a mature scar, devoid of inflammation, by approximately 8 weeks.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. 48 hours: At this early stage only basal-cell proliferation and epithelial closure are occurring, far from a mature scar.
  • B. 2 weeks: At this stage fibroblast proliferation and collagen accumulation are occurring, with Type III collagen still being replaced by Type I — the scar is not yet mature.
  • D. 6 months: Overestimates the timeline; a mature scar is already achieved by around 8 weeks in first intention healing.

posts.post_content: Healing by second intention, used for large tissue defects, is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Simple epithelial closure with no granulation tissue
Abundant granulation tissue and wound contraction

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Second intention healing occurs with extensive tissue loss (e.g. infarction, ulceration, large wounds) and is characterized by abundant granulation tissue growing from the margins as the wound contracts.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Simple epithelial closure with no granulation tissue: This describes a scenario closer to first intention healing of a small clean wound, not second intention healing of a large defect.
  • C. Complete absence of scarring: Incorrect — second intention healing typically results in an avascular, unpigmented, puckered scar without adnexa.
  • D. Healing exclusively by regeneration: Incorrect — second intention healing occurs via substitution (granulation tissue/scar formation), not simple regeneration of the original tissue.

posts.post_content: Excessive, exuberant granulation tissue that prevents wound healing is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Proud flesh" refers to exuberant granulation tissue, resulting from persistent irritation or movement, which prevents proper wound healing (especially notable in horses).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Keloid: Refers to continued connective-tissue proliferation beneath the epithelium that may recur after removal — a related but distinct entity from exuberant granulation tissue.
  • C. Fibrosarcoma: A malignant mesenchymal neoplasm; unlike proud flesh, it shows disorderly architecture rather than the orderly capillary/fibroblast pattern of granulation tissue.
  • D. Pseudomembrane: A loosely attached fibrinous exudate membrane, unrelated to granulation tissue overgrowth.

posts.post_content: PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor) primarily promotes:

_aimcq_options.text: Angiogenesis and migration/proliferation of fibroblasts, macrophages, and smooth muscle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

PDGF, released from platelets, promotes the migration and proliferation of fibroblasts, macrophages, and smooth muscle cells, along with angiogenesis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Fibrosis via collagen synthesis exclusively: This is more specifically the role of TGF-β, not PDGF's primary/exclusive function.
  • C. Mitosis of epithelial cells exclusively: This is the primary role of EGF, not PDGF.
  • D. Antiviral defence: This is the role of interferons, unrelated to PDGF's growth-promoting functions.

posts.post_content: A positive Coombs (antiglobulin) test, along with regenerative anaemia and spherocytosis, is characteristic of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is characterized by antibodies against RBC surface antigens, splenic macrophage removal of coated RBCs, regenerative anaemia, spherocytosis, and a positive Coombs test.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Myasthenia gravis: Involves autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors causing weakness, not a haemolytic anaemia picture or Coombs positivity.
  • C. Pemphigus foliaceus: Involves antibodies against epithelial glycoproteins causing bullae/acantholysis, unrelated to red blood cells.
  • D. Canine lupus erythematosus: Though it can include haemolytic anaemia among other systemic signs, the classic description of Coombs-positive regenerative anaemia with spherocytosis specifically defines autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

posts.post_content: Myasthenia gravis results from autoantibodies directed against:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Myasthenia gravis results from autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors, producing progressive weakness and low exercise tolerance.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Epithelial glycoproteins: The target in pemphigus, not myasthenia gravis.
  • C. RBC surface antigens: The target in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, not myasthenia gravis.
  • D. Thyroid follicular cells: Relevant to autoimmune thyroiditis, not myasthenia gravis.

posts.post_content: Amyloid deposits show which characteristic finding under polarised light after Congo Red staining?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Amyloid, when stained with Congo Red, shows characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarised light, reflecting its β-pleated sheet structure.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Brick-red fluorescence: This describes malignant cytoplasm under acridine orange staining in cytology, not amyloid under Congo Red.
  • C. Blue-black colouration: Describes calcium demonstrated by the von Kossa stain, not amyloid.
  • D. Yellow autofluorescence: Not the characteristic finding associated with Congo Red-stained amyloid under polarised light.

posts.post_content: AL (Amyloid Light-chain) type amyloidosis, derived from immunoglobulin light chains, is classically associated with:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains and is associated with plasmacytoma.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Chronic infectious disease: This is associated with AA amyloid (from serum amyloid associated protein), not AL amyloid.
  • C. Pancreatic islet disease: Associated with IAPP (islet amyloid polypeptide) type amyloid, not AL.
  • D. Pulmonary arterial disease: Associated with AI (apolipoprotein AI) type amyloid, not AL.

posts.post_content: Diffuse, sheet-like amyloid deposition in the spleen is grossly termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

"Bacon spleen" describes diffuse, sheet-like amyloid deposition.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Sago spleen: Describes nodular, grain-like amyloid deposition, the opposite pattern from diffuse sheet-like deposition.
  • C. Nutmeg spleen: Not a standard term used for amyloid deposition; "nutmeg" pattern is classically described for the liver in chronic venous congestion.
  • D. Tigroid spleen: Not a recognised term for amyloid deposition patterns.

posts.post_content: Deletion of self-reactive lymphocyte clones in the thymus/bone marrow, preventing autoimmunity, is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Clonal deletion, occurring in the thymus/bone marrow, represents central tolerance — the elimination of self-reactive lymphocyte clones, normally preventing autoimmune disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Peripheral tolerance: Occurs outside the primary lymphoid organs (thymus/marrow), a separate mechanism from central clonal deletion.
  • B. Clonal anergy: Refers to functional inactivation (rather than deletion) of self-reactive lymphocytes, a distinct mechanism from clonal deletion.
  • D. Molecular mimicry: A proposed mechanism by which autoimmunity can be triggered (via cross-reactive antigens), not a protective tolerance mechanism.

posts.post_content: A malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue is designated with which suffix?

Malignant epithelial tumours are designated with the suffix "-carcinoma".

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. -oma: Generally denotes a benign tumour (epithelial or mesenchymal), not a malignant one.

  • D. -blastoma: Not the standard suffix distinguishing malignant epithelial tumours in this nomenclature scheme.

posts.post_content: An intact basement membrane, with no evidence of invasion, is a feature most consistent with:

An intact basement membrane without invasion is characteristic of benign tumours.

  • D. Sarcomas exclusively: Sarcomas are malignant mesenchymal tumours and, like other malignancies, typically show invasion — not an intact basement membrane.

posts.post_content: Who was the first to identify a chemical cause of cancer (soot causing scrotal cancer in chimney sweeps)?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Sir Percival Pott (1775) was the first to identify a chemical cause of cancer, linking soot exposure to scrotal cancer in chimney sweeps.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Peyton Rous (1910): Identified the fowl sarcoma virus, a viral (not chemical) cause of cancer.
  • C. Ellerman & Bang (1908): Provided the first demonstration of viral carcinogenesis, not chemical carcinogenesis.
  • D. Yamagiwa & Ichikawa (1915): Performed experimental chemical carcinogenesis using coal tar in rabbit ears, but this was after Pott's original 1775 observation.

posts.post_content: The first demonstration of viral carcinogenesis was made by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Ellerman & Bang (1908) provided the first demonstration of viral carcinogenesis, preceding Peyton Rous's identification of the fowl sarcoma virus in 1910.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Peyton Rous (1910): Identified the fowl sarcoma virus two years after Ellerman & Bang's original demonstration, so is not the "first".
  • C. Gross (1953): Demonstrated cell-free filtrate-induced mouse leukaemia, a later contribution, not the first demonstration.
  • D. Yamagiwa & Ichikawa (1915): Worked on chemical, not viral, carcinogenesis.

posts.post_content: Spirocerca lupi infection in dogs is associated with which tumour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Spirocerca lupi infection in dogs is associated with oesophageal fibrosarcoma/osteosarcoma as a parasite-induced neoplastic change.

  • A. Bile duct tumour: Associated instead with Eimeria stiedae infection in rabbits, not Spirocerca lupi in dogs.

posts.post_content: Carcinomas typically metastasize predominantly via which route?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Carcinomas typically spread via the lymphatic route.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Haematogenous spread: This is the typical route for sarcomas, not carcinomas.
  • C. Transcoelomic spread: A distinct mechanism (lack of cell cohesiveness allowing seeding in body cavities, the "soil theory"), seen classically in ovarian/gastric cancer, not the predominant route for carcinomas in general.
  • D. Direct inoculation only: Refers to a specific mechanism (e.g. canine transmissible venereal tumour), not the general/predominant route for carcinomas.

TSAs are unique mutated proteins presented via MHC I and recognised by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

posts.post_content: Cancer cachexia, characterized by wasting and appetite suppression, is primarily driven by:

Cancer cachexia is primarily driven by TNF-α, which suppresses appetite and inhibits lipoprotein lipase activity, resulting in wasting and negative nitrogen balance.

posts.post_content: In the TNM staging system, the "N" component refers to:

In the TNM system, "N" denotes nodal (lymph node) involvement (N0 = none, N1 = regional node, N2 = distant node).
